text: Great breakdown. The promotional zero fee works exactly like a bank’s teaser rate on a savings account: a great price to bring new money in, then a normal price once you’re settled. Providers know that most people never move again, because moving costs something: time, the spread on selling and buying, and outside an ISA, possibly tax on the gain. So the question isn’t only what the fee is today. It’s what the fee will be in three years, when leaving is no longer free.

Yes - there is a little rule that says if you own individual USA shares inside a SIPP you have no witholding taxes. But this does not apply to funds. So in practice it's not quite as useful as buying a broad market index fund.
@TobyNewbatt Ah yes useful to know. I have my US dividends in pies so never had to look into it for funds. Thanks.

4:22 Would the transaction cost not be a one-time cost when purchasing or selling the ETF? As oppose to the OCF which is charged annually for the duration of the period you hold the fund. So adding them together to get the "true" cost isn't really applicable as you only pay the transaction cost twice for any given unit you hold but the OCF you could pay 30+ times depending how long you hold the asset. If I'm mistaken about the nature of the transaction cost then please correct me.

The transaction costs relate to the internal trading costs the fund incurs to keep up with it's index replication, so it is ongoing. A big part of those transaction costs is the bid offer spread of the individual shares being bought to replicate the index.

The one-off you're referring to is the bid offer spread you pay when buying/selling your ETF shares.

There's no withholding tax in pensions. I guess it mean that holding ETFs in SIPP incurs additional tax that you wouldn't pay by holding shares directly?

Withholding tax has nothing to do with the account it’s being held in. It’s a tax taken by the US government from any non US nationals who hold shares. You never see the money it never reaches your account here in the UK or the fund you are invested in 👍

​ @TobyNewbatt  You're wrong, this is determined by UK-US Double Taxation Treaty and pension holdings are treated differently from ordinary accounts or ISAs. You sign W8BEN form and if you hold shares in a SIPP they don't deduct the tax.

@antych Yes, 0% US withholding tax is one of the benefits a pension can have compared with other types of accounts. 

To get this applied, an W-8BEN isn’t going to be required for, say, an AJ Bell SIPP when the scheme itself is the beneficial owner of the bought shares. Hence they state one is not required to be completed by the SIPP customer.
@adrianl5899 Correct - Just to mention that this only applies to US shares held individually - this does not apply to ETFs they still are hit with the 15% witholding tax

If that zero fee ETF is receiving dividends (or the swap value of the dividends) then presumably someone somewhere will also be paying the 15% withholding tax (or 30% if domiciled outside Ireland). So that should be counted as a (hidden) cost of holding that ETF, as it is with VUSA.
If the zero fee ETF never receives dividends (or the swap value of the dividends) at all then presumably it would be losing 0.85% against VUSA (assuming an annual SP500 dividend of 1%), which is much worse.
Either way, the comparison chart at 8:56 seems to be off.
Personally I think that swap and sampled index-tracking ETFs are an unnecessary complexity, at least for major indices. For me the whole point of an index-tracking ETF is to get full physical replication of the index. I always prefer to actually own the thing I buy, rather than just some token of it. So for that reason alone I would buy VUSA rather than the zero-fee ETF.

You’ve misunderstood things here. The swap agreement gets the fund the full total return of the index they are tracking….it avoids withholding tax. That’s the whole point. Dividends are part of the total return of an index.

The counterparty doesn’t have to pay withholding tax - for example they could be based in the US or have a mechanism that means they don’t pay the tax.

@TobyNewbatt I understand that and dividends are indeed part of the total return, but is that what this zero fee ETF is really matching? Or is it just matching the price index excluding paid dividends? I don't see this clearly stated on their website and so far there is no way to compare the price of the ETF and the index over time as the ETF is new.
The price index excluding dividends is what one normally sees when looking at an index on a financial news or stockbroker website, with some of them giving the option to include dividends for comparison purposes. Hence my doubt.
Either way, the whole idea of tracking an index without physically owning its constituent parts seems inherently insecure to me. Probably OK as long as markets are stable, but could go badly wrong if they destabilise. On their own website they say that they may not actually manage to do what they intend and if they don't then the level of fees will be the last thing to worry about!
I will stick to ETFs with physical replication and low fees.
Interesting video anyway. Thanks.
